If you change this line you might just as well print strerror(errno) too.

This could print "(date): getaddrinfo(host) returned The requested socket type is not supported". That looks a bit unfamiilar. Can't you just stick to the classic layout of "${function}: ${error cause}" rather than "${function} returned ${error cause}".

This is done by `perror(buf)` which immediately prints `buf+strerror(errno)` to stderr. It seems the difference between `perror(buf)` and `fprintf(stderr, "%s: %s", buf, strerror(errno))` is that the former is thread-safe and the later not. I would rather stick with the thread-safe variant for now.

I personally don't like the "chaining" using ':' like this: "${date}: ${function}: ${error cause}: {system error}". For me the ':' have different meanings. The first means "happend at", the second "failed because", the third "this also belongs to this error". In writing this I realize that there is a better solution (although it may not be thread-safe). I'll change the PR shortly.

Shouldn't this be done inside the foreach loop? If multiple files have the same type of error only the last file will be reported because $*_error is overwritten each time and only reported outside the foreach loop.

What exactly does "this" refer to?

The xml_error() actually terminates the function and thus the loop. If the xml_error() call is inside the loop, it is terminated after the first error, and other ("later") uploaded files aren't deleted and would stay in the temp directory forever. One could argue, though, that in case of one error _all_ files uploaded with the request need to be deleted immediately from the filesystem and the DB, but this would make it even more complicated.

Then again, though, the loop should probably go over all actually uploaded files in $_FILES rather than the list of md5s in the request, but that would mean a complete re-write of upload_files().

"this" refers to the three if statements on line 200ff. 

Use-Case: uploading two files (file1.zip, file2.zip) which both could not be moved to the download directory. Because of line 181 which is called once for each file, $move_error at the end (on line 200) only contains "could not move /tmp/file2.zip to download/*/file2.zip" thus hiding the error with file1.zip

A quick fix would be to initialize `$*_error` with an empty string. Concatenating the error messages and checking for `strlen($*_error)>0` in the if blocks at the end.

To catch all errors one could also only use one `$error_str` variable and concatenate the errors to it and call xml_error() only once reporting all the errors that happened.

Oops, I was mistaken. get_project_config_poll does always reply with `<project_config>` even in case of an error. But the same is not true for lookup_account_poll which replies with `<error>` instead of `<account_out>`.

The logic now is to look for `<account_out` if that is present return the string starting from there. If it is not present look for `<error` and return the string from there (which can produce malformed XML because you do not check if the closing tag matches). If this is also not found return an empty `<account_out/>`. This `<error>` output is also not consistent with the other two functions you mentioned. Do the other two RPCs not report an error?

The error reporting is inconsistent. `get_project_config_poll` returns errors like this:

```
<project_config>
    <error_num>%d</error_num>
</project_config>
```

No special handling required here. `lookup_account_poll` returns

```
<account_out>
  <error_num>%d</error_num>
</account_out>
```

in case of a client-side error (e.g. GetHostByName) and

```
<error>
  <error_num>%d</error_num>
  <error_msg>%s</error_msg>
</error>
```

in case of a server-side error (e.g. DBNotFound). `get_all_projects_list` again does not have any error reporting at all and returns an empty response in the unlikely case that all_projects_list.xml cannot be read.

This is why there's special handling of `<error>` in `lookup_account_poll`.

Why are you now checking if `topic->timestamp != 0` when before it was a string comparison? I would expect from the name and the previous comparison that this contains an actual timestamp if the topic is not new.

It's a hacky solution to the problem, `$topic->timestamp` is a string which is either blank (empty) or ==`new`. The problem is that `new` is translated into a language, example `neu`, by drupal. Therefore a string comparison won't work.

Thus my solution is to simply check the existence of `$topic->timestamp`. If the topic is not new, then the field should be empty.

This and `choose_teams()` is compensating for the lack of a proper SQL JOIN clause implemented in `BoincCreditUser` for this use-case with several DB calls to eliminate old entries (mainly for the teams). Thus it would make more sense to me to write a custom `BoincCreditUser::get_list($where_clause, $order_clause, $limit)` function which does something like 
```
SELECT * from user u join user_credit cu on u.id=cu.userid where $where_clause order by $order_clause limit $limit
```
This will eliminate the need to check if a user or team still exists (because that is not part of the returned list) reducing the amount of queries per call.

The BOINC-GAHP server will only have a default if it was read from a config file, which I think was implemented for easier testing. Either we should completely specify the config file (name, location, contents) or be completely silent about it in the specification. IMHO the config file is part of the GAHP daemon implementation, not of the protocol. Conformant to the protocol not having specified a BOINC project should result in an error, even if a config file is present.

Right now there is no sequence requirement specified in section 3.4 so `BOINC_SELECT_PROJECT` is optional and other commands should fail when no config file is present. The current implementation is using an uninitialized char array if no config file is present and no `BOINC_SELECT_PROJECT` command was received. The values are not further checked in the remote submit API and directly used.

If we make it mandatory then there is no need for a config file. If we allow `NULL` as `project_url` and `authenticator` to signal the server to use a config file then we need to add the `F` return value so the server can signal to the client that there is no config file thus still no project selected.

I don't think we need to specify the config file in the protocol just that the server may implement a way to have a default project already configured that eliminates an initial `BOINC_SELECT_PROJECT` because all users on the condor site should use the same BOINC account but you don't want to give them the authenticator.

>  The current implementation is using an uninitialized char array if no config file is present and no BOINC_SELECT_PROJECT command was received.

This is a bug (in the implementation, not in the protocol) and should be fixed. However, *how* it should be fixed should be specified in the protocol. If the config file is an officially supported option, it should be fully specified in the protocol.

As we found out the `t()` or `bts()` function needs to be called at least once for a non-english language so that the string gets added to the Drupal Translation Interface (DTI). This means that the project that is providing the canonical translation templates for Drupal needs to visit each webpage on its site to ensure that every string is added to the DTI and thus is part of the exported template. The comment suggests that some static string extractor is used which is not the case for the "boinc" and "project" textgroups currently. For projects importing translations this is not a problem as those get added to the DTI automatically.

While I always add curly braces (`{}`) around all variables in shell code *I* write, doing so is only required when doing any kind of variable substitution (ie: `${ANDROID_TC_X86:-Default}`). In practice you'll find lots and lots of shell code that only uses the braces when required and this won't cause any problems if you always consider wether the character *after* the variable name *may be part of a shell variable name* or not when writing it.

I tend to ofter *not* consider the above criterion in practice so I add the braces just to be safe, but this really only matters when you write the code; once it's properly written adding the braces everywhere is really not worth the (wasted) time, while also likely to cause hard to spot errors if the code is not reviewed very carefully (wasting everybody's time).

This code is the first time that BOINC uses session.  Up to this point, the website has been essentially stateless (i.e. all information needed to support the request is contained on the request or loaded from the database based on information in the request).  I have two questions about this.

1) Do any BOINC projects do load balancing using more than one web server to serve their site?  If not, then question 2 isn't important.
2) Are we expecting BOINC projects that have more than one web server to use some form of server affinity?

If there is a project using load balancing between servers, then caching the data in the session could become problematic if the users request winds up on a server that doesn't have this data cached.  

This is a pretty big architectural decision to go from stateless to stateful requests.  Perhaps it would be better to store the data you are putting in the session in a temp cookie so that we don't make this change now.

I admit I did not think of the high-level implications of using a stateful architecture when writing this.

I (obviously) need some kind of temporary space to store the user information  while traversing multiple pages, so the SESSION seemed like an obvious candidate. I have used it on occasion for Drupal-Web development.

But if the same functionality can be made with a temporary cookie, then I'll refactor this section of the code.
